subject: history

moments.title: Runnymede
moments.body: After military failures in France (loss of Normandy 1204) and heavy taxation, the barons rebelled. At Runnymede on 15 June 1215, John attached his seal to the Articles of the Barons. The fuller Charter of Liberties (Magna Carta) followed within days.

quote.text: No free man shall be seized or imprisoned... except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land.

moments.takeaway: Clauses 39 and 40 are the source of due process traditions. Most of the original 63 clauses are about specific feudal grievances — fish-weirs, forest law, scutage.

moments.title: Annulled by the Pope
moments.body: On 24 August 1215, Pope Innocent III's bull declares Magna Carta 'null and void of all validity forever'. Civil war resumes; the barons invite Prince Louis of France to take the throne.
moments.takeaway: Magna Carta failed in 1215 as a peace treaty. Its reissues (1216, 1217, 1225, 1297) under Henry III and Edward I are what survived.

now.title: Foundational myth and real law
now.body: Three clauses of the 1297 reissue remain on English statute books today, including clause 29 (descended from clause 39). Magna Carta as 'foundation of liberty' is largely the construction of Sir Edward Coke in the 17th century, used against the Stuarts. The US founders cited it constantly. Four original 1215 copies survive — two at the British Library, one each at Lincoln and Salisbury cathedrals.
now.open_questions: How much of Magna Carta is rhetoric versus law? Sir James Holt's 'Magna Carta' (1965, 1992) treats it both as a baronial treaty of its moment and as a document whose later use was not accidental — the framers genuinely tried to bind the crown.

reflection: A failed 13th-century peace treaty became, by deliberate later use, the symbolic charter of constitutional government. Both the original failure and the later reinvention are part of its meaning.
